title: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams 1986
text:
CHAPTER 13. BACKPROPAGATION AND CONNECTIONISM
SECTION 13.2. RUMELHART, HINTON AND WILLIAMS, 1986

On 9 October 1986, Nature published a four-page letter, "Learning representations by back-propagating errors," by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams (volume 323, pages 533-536). The same year, the two-volume book "Parallel Distributed Processing" by Rumelhart, James McClelland and the PDP Research Group appeared, containing a longer chapter by the same three authors, "Learning Internal Representations by Error Propagation." The algorithm was not new (Section 13.1 traced its earlier history), but these publications made it the standard way to train multilayer networks and launched the second wave of neural network research. This section explains what the 1986 work showed, why it was persuasive, what came with it (Hopfield networks, Boltzmann machines, connectionism), and what its limits were.

1. The people and the PDP group

David Rumelhart (1942-2011) was a cognitive psychologist at the University of California, San Diego (UCSD), interested in how people understand language and stories. With James McClelland he led the Parallel Distributed Processing (PDP) research group at UCSD's Institute for Cognitive Science in the early 1980s. Geoffrey Hinton, a British-born researcher with a PhD in artificial intelligence from Edinburgh, worked with the group at UCSD after finding it hard to get funding in Britain, then moved to Carnegie Mellon and, in 1987, to Toronto (the University of Toronto and the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research). Ronald Williams was a member of the PDP group from 1983 to 1986 and later did influential work on recurrent networks and reinforcement learning (the REINFORCE algorithm, 1992) at Northeastern University.

According to accounts of the history, Rumelhart rediscovered the backpropagation idea around 1982, independently of Werbos, and the group developed it into a practical method. The 1985 technical report and the 1986 papers did not cite Werbos's 1974 dissertation, which was little known at the time; David Parker and Yann LeCun (in his 1985-1987 work in France) also described versions of the method independently. Credit for backpropagation is therefore spread across many people over two decades. What the 1986 work added decisively was demonstration and interpretation.

2. The Nature paper's argument

The paper's title emphasized representations. Its key claim was that backpropagation makes the hidden units learn to represent important features of the task domain, features not specified by the designer, and that this overcomes the limitation of perceptrons identified by Minsky and Papert (Section 10.3). The paper described the generalized delta rule: the LMS rule extended to multilayer networks of units with smooth, nonlinear (sigmoid) activations, with error signals propagated backward through the weights, exactly the procedure worked out in Section 13.1:

    delta_j = (t_j - y_j) * f'(net_j)                  for output units
    delta_j = f'(net_j) * sum_k delta_k * w_kj          for hidden units
    Delta w_ji = eta * delta_j * y_i                    (plus a momentum term)

They also used a momentum term to speed learning,

    Delta w(n) = -eta * dE/dw(n) + alpha * Delta w(n-1),   0 <= alpha < 1

which averages successive gradients and damps oscillation in narrow valleys of the error surface. Momentum is still used, in one form or another, in essentially every modern optimizer.

Demonstrations. The 1986 papers showed networks discovering internal representations on small, carefully designed problems, including (as described in the papers and widely summarized):

  - XOR and parity: the canonical problems that a single-layer perceptron cannot solve. A network with a hidden layer learned them, refuting the practical force of the single-layer limitation (though not the deeper scaling issues Minsky and Papert had raised).
  - Symmetry detection: deciding whether a binary input pattern is symmetric about its center. A network with just two hidden units learned an elegant solution, with weights mirror-symmetric in magnitude and opposite in sign, arranged in ratios so that only perfectly symmetric patterns produce zero net input.
  - Family trees: a network learned relationships (father, aunt and so on) in two isomorphic family trees, one English and one Italian. Inspection of the hidden units showed they had learned features such as nationality, generation and branch of the family, without being told about them. This is an early example of learned distributed representations, the ancestor of word embeddings (Chapter 17).
  - Encoder problems: compressing N one-hot patterns through log2(N) hidden units and reconstructing them, discovering binary-like codes (the idea behind autoencoders).

The family tree example especially mattered. It showed that a neural network could learn structured, relational knowledge in a distributed form, the kind of knowledge that symbolic AI had represented with explicit rules and that expert systems had needed knowledge engineers to supply (Chapter 12).

3. The surrounding revival

Backpropagation was the center of a larger revival in the early-to-mid 1980s.

Hopfield networks (1982). The physicist John Hopfield showed that a network of binary threshold units with symmetric connections (w_ij = w_ji) has an energy function

    E = -(1/2) sum_(i,j) w_ij s_i s_j + sum_i theta_i s_i

that never increases when units are updated asynchronously. The network therefore settles into local minima of E, which can be made to store memories: with the Hebbian rule w_ij = sum over patterns of s_i s_j (Section 7.3), presenting a corrupted pattern causes the network to fall into the nearest stored pattern. Such content-addressable memory can store about 0.14 N random patterns in N units before recall breaks down (a classic result from statistical physics). Hopfield's work attracted physicists to the field and gave neural networks mathematical respectability.

Boltzmann machines (1983-1985). Hinton and Terry Sejnowski (with David Ackley in the 1985 paper) made Hopfield-style networks stochastic: each unit turns on with probability s(net input / T) at "temperature" T, borrowing simulated annealing. They derived a learning rule for networks with hidden units based on differences between correlations when the visible units are clamped to data and when the network runs freely:

    Delta w_ij = eta * (<s_i s_j>_data - <s_i s_j>_model)

It was elegant and connected to statistical mechanics, but slow, because estimating the model correlations required long sampling. A restricted form (restricted Boltzmann machines) became important later in the deep learning story (Chapter 16). Sejnowski reportedly tried both Boltzmann learning and backpropagation for NETtalk and found backpropagation much faster.

In 2024, John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton received the Nobel Prize in Physics for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks, recognizing this line of work. Hinton, Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCun had received the 2018 ACM Turing Award for conceptual and engineering breakthroughs that made deep neural networks a critical component of computing.

NETtalk (1987). Terry Sejnowski and Charles Rosenberg trained a network with backpropagation to convert English text into a stream of phonemes, which drove a DECtalk speech synthesizer. In the commonly described configuration, the input was a window of seven letters, the output was the phoneme for the middle letter, and the hidden layer had 80 units. As training progressed, the synthesized speech went from babbling to recognizable words, and recordings of this were widely played, giving the public a vivid picture of a machine learning to read aloud. DECtalk itself converted text to phonemes with hand-written rules; NETtalk's point was that comparable mappings could be learned from examples alone.

The PDP books. "Parallel Distributed Processing: Explorations in the Microstructure of Cognition" (MIT Press, 1986), in two volumes, collected models of perception, memory, language and learning. One chapter, Rumelhart and McClelland's model of learning English past tenses, learned to produce regular and irregular forms (including overregularization errors like "goed" that children make) without explicit rules, and provoked a long debate with linguists Steven Pinker and Alan Prince, who argued (1988) that the model failed to capture key properties of language.

Connectionism. The PDP group's broader program, connectionism, held that cognition emerges from the interaction of many simple units with knowledge stored in connection weights, as opposed to the symbolic view that cognition is rule-governed manipulation of symbols (the physical symbol system hypothesis, Section 9.1). Jerry Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn (1988) argued that connectionist networks could not explain the systematic, compositional structure of thought (if you can think "John loves Mary" you can think "Mary loves John") unless they implemented a symbol system. This debate continues in a new form in 2026, about whether large language models genuinely generalize compositionally.

4. Why 1986 and not 1974?

Backpropagation had been described before, so why did the 1986 version take off?

  - Demonstration: the papers showed working networks learning interesting internal representations, not just an equation.
  - Interpretation: the framing in terms of learned representations addressed the main objection to perceptrons directly and connected with cognitive psychology.
  - Community: the PDP books gave a whole research program, with models, software and a large audience in psychology, neuroscience and computer science.
  - Computers: workstations of the mid-1980s could run small networks interactively; in the early 1970s this was much harder.
  - Timing: symbolic AI was approaching the expert systems bust (Section 11.2), and researchers were open to alternatives.

5. What followed, and the limits

Applications came quickly in the late 1980s and early 1990s: handwritten digit recognition (Section 13.3), speech recognition components, financial prediction, process control, and the ALVINN system (Dean Pomerleau, Carnegie Mellon, around 1989), which used a small backpropagation network to steer a vehicle from camera images. Theoretical results showed that a network with one hidden layer of sigmoid units can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region to arbitrary accuracy, given enough hidden units (the universal approximation theorem: George Cybenko, 1989; Kurt Hornik and colleagues, 1989).

But by the mid-1990s, enthusiasm faded again. Problems:

  - Deep networks (many layers) were very hard to train with sigmoid units because of vanishing gradients (Section 13.1). Most practical networks had one or two hidden layers.
  - Training was slow on the computers of the time, and required careful tuning of learning rates, initialization and architecture, a "black art."
  - Datasets were small, so large networks overfit.
  - Results were hard to interpret.
  - Competing methods, especially support vector machines (from the early-to-mid 1990s), had convex training with a unique solution, strong theory and often equal or better accuracy on the datasets of the day (Chapter 14).

From the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s, neural networks were again a minority approach in machine learning. A small number of groups, notably those of Hinton (Toronto), LeCun (Bell Labs, later New York University), Bengio (Montreal) and Jürgen Schmidhuber (Switzerland), kept working on them. When large labeled datasets, GPUs and some technical improvements arrived around 2006-2012, the same backpropagation algorithm became the engine of deep learning (Chapters 15-16).

6. Summary

  - Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams published "Learning representations by back-propagating errors" in Nature on 9 October 1986, with a longer chapter in the PDP books the same year.
  - They presented the generalized delta rule with momentum and showed hidden units learning useful representations: XOR and parity, symmetry detection, encoders, and family-tree relations.
  - Backpropagation had earlier independent discoverers (Linnainmaa, Werbos, Parker, LeCun and others); the 1986 work's contribution was demonstration, interpretation and community.
  - The revival also included Hopfield networks (1982), Boltzmann machines (1983-1985), NETtalk (1987) and the connectionism debate.
  - Hopfield and Hinton received the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics; Hinton, Bengio and LeCun the 2018 Turing Award.
  - Training deep networks remained difficult until the late 2000s, and SVMs overtook neural networks in the 1990s.
